data.body_html:
Packing for a yacht charter in Marbella in 2038 is simpler than you think — but a few essentials make the difference between a good day and a great one. Whether you’re cruising from Puerto Banús to Cabopino, Estepona, or Sotogrande, this checklist covers clothing, sun protection, tech, and hidden costs like port fees. All our charters include a licensed skipper, fuel, drinks, snacks, insurance, and 21% VAT — so you can leave the logistics to us. Here’s what to bring for a seamless 8-hour trip on the Costa del Sol.

Clothing and Footwear

Light, breathable fabrics win on the Mediterranean. In July and August, air temps hit 33°C and sea temps 24°C. Pack a swimsuit, a cover-up, and a light jacket or windbreaker for the evening return — the breeze picks up after 6pm. No hard-soled shoes on deck: barefoot or non-marking soles only. Flip-flops are fine; boat shoes are better. If you plan to walk to a beach club (e.g., Nikki Beach or Ocean Club), bring trainers for the short stroll from the anchorage.

Sun Protection and Health Essentials

Marbella’s sun is intense — UV index 9+ from May to September. Bring reef-safe sun cream (oxybenzone-free) to comply with Marbella’s 2030 eco-bylaw; brands like Riemann P20 SPF50 or Green People SPF30 are sold at supermarkets in Puerto Banús. A wide-brimmed hat, polarised sunglasses, and a lip balm with SPF are non-negotiable. If you’re prone to motion sickness, take Kwells or Stugeron 30 minutes before departure — the Mediterranean is calm, but a few guests feel the swell near Cabo Pino.

Tech and Entertainment

Most boats have Bluetooth stereos, but a portable speaker in a dry bag is fine. Charge your phone and camera beforehand — power outlets are limited on smaller boats like the Dubhe (8m, 5 pax) or Mariah SX21. A waterproof phone pouch (€10 at Decathlon) lets you take photos from the swim platform. Download offline maps of Marbella and Estepona; mobile signal is strong near the coast but patchy in coves like Cala del Faro or Cala Cortés.

Documents and Payments

Every passenger needs a passport or national ID card. The crew may request a copy 24h before departure for the manifest. No visa needed for EU citizens; non-EU guests should check Spanish entry rules. Bring a card or cash for port fees — these are not included in the charter price. Typical costs: Cabopino €50–€80, Estepona €80–€120, Sotogrande €100–€150. If you want to stop at a beach club, budget €20–€50 per person for loungers and drinks.

Food and Drink

Every charter includes water, soft drinks, beer, white wine, cava, and light snacks (crisps, olives, nuts). For longer trips, pre-order a catering platter via WhatsApp: €25–€45 per person for cold meats, cheese, fruit, or sushi. No outside food is allowed unless pre-arranged — the crew needs to manage waste and allergens. If you have dietary restrictions, tell us 48h in advance and we’ll adjust the snacks.

What NOT to Bring

  • Hard luggage: No suitcases or large bags — space is limited. Use a soft duffel or backpack.
  • Glass bottles: Most charters ban glass on deck for safety. Use plastic or metal reusable bottles.
  • Illegal substances: Spanish law is strict. The crew will terminate the charter and call the port police if drugs are found.
  • Pets: Only allowed on private charters with prior approval. Check via WhatsApp before booking.

Seasonal Adjustments for 2038

Summer 2038 is expected to be hotter than average, with July highs of 35°C. Pack extra water (though we provide it). Spring and autumn trips (April–May, September–October) need a light jumper or fleece — sea breezes drop to 18°C after sunset. Winter charters (November–March) are rare but possible on the Azimut 58 Flybridge (17.6m, 12 pax); bring a waterproof jacket and warm layers.
